meta.title: SQLLens: see where your database breaks before you write code
meta.description: Paste SQL. SQLLens draws the real B-Tree of your table, pits two sessions against each other for locks and lists the risks with evidence.

hero.lead: Paste SQL. SQLLens draws the real B-Tree of your table, pits two sessions against each other for locks and lists the risks with evidence.
hero.note: PostgreSQL runs right in your browser. MySQL and the AI Mentor need a sign-in.
hero.treeLabel: Sample B-Tree: a key travels from the root down to a leaf and then to the heap
hero.caption: A sample tree, the numbers are examples. In SQLLens this is the real tree of your table.

descent.title: A key travels from root to leaf
descent.lead: For each lookup, PostgreSQL reads exactly one page per level and then jumps to the heap for the row. Watch key 7421 go down.
descent.listLabel: The steps of one key lookup
descent.s1: Start at the root. The root has one boundary, 5000, and 7421 is larger, so go right.
descent.s2: The internal page has the boundary 7500. 7421 is smaller, so take its left child.
descent.s3: This leaf holds the keys from 5000 to 7499, so 7421 is here. The index returns the location of the row.
descent.s4: The index is stored apart from the table, so the last step jumps to the heap for the real row. Four pages in total.
descent.note: This is a sample tree. In SQLLens it is the real tree of your table, read with pageinspect and labelled Real.

race.title: Data grows, the index still reads about as many pages
race.lead: One question: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42, returning 10 rows. A full scan reads more pages with every row added, while going through the index barely moves.
race.seq: Seq Scan, read the whole table
race.idx: Index Scan, go through the index
race.context: Measured in Chromium with PGlite 0.5.14 and PostgreSQL 18.6 on 2026-11-02, median of 3 runs. Page counts are shared hit plus read from the top Buffers line of EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). The indexed query was planned by the planner as a Bitmap Heap Scan. SQLLens compares page counts, not sandbox run times.

lock.title: Two sessions hold each other's locks
lock.lead: No single statement is wrong. The failure only shows when two sessions run together, each holding what the other needs.
lock.listLabel: The steps of the deadlock scenario
lock.s1: Session A updates the row with id = 1 and holds its lock.
lock.s2: Session B updates the row with id = 2 and holds its lock.
lock.s3: Session A updates the row with id = 2. B holds that lock, so A has to wait.
lock.s4: Session B updates the row with id = 1. A holds that lock, so B waits for A while A waits for B. The two wait on each other in a loop.
lock.s5: PostgreSQL detects the loop and aborts one of the two sessions. Which one is aborted is not fixed, so SQLLens does not guess.
lock.context: The SQLLens conflict-sim model matches real PostgreSQL 18 on 13 variants of the 5 scenarios, checked by hand. This is one of those five scenarios.

scale.title: Scale the data up and the tree grows a level
scale.lead: With more data a single page can no longer hold every boundary, and the root splits into a new level. The number of levels also depends on key width: this is an index on a column of the measured table.
scale.s3: 500,000 rows: level 2, the root split into an internal level, index 4,640 KB.
scale.s4: Above 500,000 rows SQLLens does not run for real. Levels and size come from a formula.
scale.estNote: The formula was checked against real PostgreSQL 18: a 500,000-row sample extrapolated to 5,000,000 rows for int, text and uuid indexes gave the right number of levels and a size off by no more than 0.14%. It holds only for indexes built with CREATE INDEX, and has not been checked on indexes bloated by UPDATE or DELETE.
scale.realNote: Measured in Chromium with PGlite 0.5.14 on 2026-11-02.
scale.treeLabel: A B-Tree gaining a level as the row count grows

labels.title: Every conclusion carries exactly one label
labels.lead: You always know where a number came from.
labels.realBody: The database just produced this result. B-Trees read with pageinspect and page counts from EXPLAIN are this kind.
labels.simBody: Computed by the project's own engine and checked against a real database. The contention scenarios on PostgreSQL are this kind.
labels.estBody: Extrapolated beyond the size that can be run. Above 500,000 rows only this kind exists.

limits.title: What SQLLens does not say
limits.l1: It never says your design is fine. It only says: under this assumption, this scenario breaks or does not break at this step.
limits.l2: It does not predict production. Run time in a sandbox is not run time on your machine, so it compares only by rows and pages read.
limits.l3: It does not guess what it cannot simulate. Where it cannot, it says so: not simulated yet.
